claims.text: Integrating machine-learning interatomic potentials with two-phase coexistence or the Z method can accurately predict melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting for high-melting refractory materials.
The proposed ML-driven framework significantly reduces computational cost relative to full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The modeled refractory material is initially a high-temperature solid near its melting transition.
Full DFT-based molecular dynamics can be replaced by an ML interatomic potential coupled to two-phase coexistence or the Z method.
The simulations must operate near the melting point where solid and liquid phases can be sampled.
An ML potential trained on suitable configurations can capture DFT-level accuracy.
The ML-trained potential reproduces the DFT-level energy and force landscapes governing atomic-scale interactions.
ML potentials reduce computational expense by approximating DFT energies and forces.
Two-phase coexistence or the Z method can efficiently sample melting transitions without full thermodynamic integration.
The predicted melting properties will closely agree with full DFT calculations and available experimental data.
The proposed predictions can be obtained using a fraction of the computational cost of full DFT calculations.
Conventional ab initio free-energy methods based on DFT molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration are accurate.
Conventional ab initio free-energy methods are computationally prohibitive for high-throughput screening.
The proposed method should perform well when the ML potential is trained on representative configurations near melting.
Accuracy may deteriorate when complex phase behavior or defect-induced variations fall outside the ML training regime.
Incomplete coverage of high-temperature dynamics or extreme-condition behavior in the training data introduces uncertainty in the predictions.
A deviation greater than 5% from full DFT results or experimental data is proposed as a falsification threshold.
Failure to significantly reduce computational cost would falsify the hypothesis.
